title: The Hare in the Moon
text:
In this tale of one of the Buddha's earlier lives, he was born as a wise hare living in a forest with three friends: a monkey, a jackal and an otter. The hare taught them to keep the holy days and to give food to anyone who asked.

On one holy day each friend went looking for something to give. The otter found fish left on a river bank, the jackal found some meat and a pot of curds, and the monkey picked mangoes. The hare had only grass, and nobody eats grass. So he decided that if a beggar came, he would give his own body.

Sakka, king of the gods, heard of this resolve and came down disguised as a hungry brahmin. The others gave him their food. When he reached the hare, the hare told him to light a fire. Then the hare shook himself three times so that no small creature in his fur would die with him, and leapt into the flames.

The fire did not burn him; it felt cool as snow. Sakka revealed himself and, so that the hare's goodness would be remembered for an age, pressed a mountain to squeeze out its essence and drew the outline of a hare on the face of the moon.
lesson: Generosity is measured by what it costs the giver, not by the size of the gift. Give what you truly have, even if it seems small.
people: The Bodhisatta as a hare, Sakka
